children: PSBs raised $13.4 billion through FCNR(B) deposits, exceeding targets as Bank of Baroda led mobilisation under the RBI’s special swap facility

Public sector banks have substantially exceeded their initial fundraising targets under the Reserve Bank of India’s special FCNR(B) deposit window, as overseas depositors responded strongly to the concessional swap facility. Bank of Baroda mobilised around USD 8 billion, nearly double its initial USD 4-5 billion target.

Bank of India raised about USD 2.33 billion, against a target of USD 1.2 billion, while Central Bank of India mobilised around USD 760 million, compared with its original USD 400 million target. Indian Bank also raised around USD 2.3 billion through the facility.

The mobilisation came as banks tapped the RBI’s special USD-INR swap facility, which generated USD 127.22 billion through FCNR(B) deposits by August 31. Total inflows across FCNR(B) deposits, overseas foreign currency borrowings and external commercial borrowings reached USD 136.37 billion.
Banks Focus On Replacing Costlier Funding

Banks are looking to use the funds to reduce dependence on expensive domestic funding while gradually supporting credit growth. Bank of Baroda expects the FCNR(B) inflows to replace around Rs 17,000-18,000 crore of bulk deposits. Bank of India is also prioritising the replacement of high-cost bulk deposits and maturing bonds, while maintaining its credit-growth guidance of 15-17 per cent.

Indian Bank plans to deploy its mobilisation towards rupee liquidity, lending and reducing reliance on bulk deposits. The RBI had originally allowed fresh FCNR(B) mobilisation under the concessional swap facility until September 30. However, after mobilisation reached USD 52.3 billion by August 13, the central bank advanced the closure of the window to August 31, citing the strong response and resultant foreign-exchange inflows.

The large inflows have also raised questions about how quickly banks can deploy the funds without putting pressure on lending spreads. SBI Chairman Challa Sreenivasulu Setty said banks could take three to four months to deploy the liquidity and cautioned against abnormal lending. For public sector banks, the immediate benefit is expected to come from replacing higher-cost liabilities, while incremental lending is likely to build gradually through FY27.
